A third-rank holder in his MBBS course, he had chosen Maharashtra for postgraduate training, hoping to build his career in the state. On Saturday, Patil was found dead in a hospital bathroom after reportedly injecting himself with an anaesthetic drug.

He had been on duty for nearly 11 hours, with his shift scheduled to continue until midnight.“He would enthusiastically tell me about his daily achievements. ‘Pappa, I got to perform a minor surgery today.

Pappa, I got to do this today,’” his father, Mallikarjun Patil, a chemist from Yadgir district in Karnataka, told The Indian Express. But Patil also spoke to his father about the workload and stress he faced at the hospital.
According to Mallikarjun, his son felt intimidated by senior doctors and would rush to the hospital at odd hours whenever they messaged him, fearing that any delay would affect how they viewed him.

He would leave without even brushing his teeth or showering, his father recalled. On some days, he began work at 8 am and returned home after 1 am. Signs of exhaustion had emerged nearly three months earlier.

articles.dek: The Central Bureau of Investigation has arrested four individuals in connection with a scheme where impersonators took exams for public sector bank jobs, using iris scans to identify discrepancies.
articles.lead: The Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) revealed in a Mumbai special court that iris scan matches exposed a racket involving "dummy candidates" taking exams for public sector banks. The CBI alleges that scans conducted during examinations across various states matched arrested individuals who were not the actual candidates seeking employment.
articles.takeaway: The Central Bureau of Investigation has arrested four individuals in connection with a scheme where impersonators took exams for public sector bank jobs, using iris scans to identify discrepancies.
body: The Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) revealed in a Mumbai special court that iris scan matches exposed a racket involving "dummy candidates" taking exams for public sector banks. The CBI alleges that scans conducted during examinations across various states matched arrested individuals who were not the actual candidates seeking employment.

The scheme involved impersonators appearing for recruitment exams held between 2020 and 2024 for public sector banks and regional rural banks, facilitated by the Institute of Banking Personnel Selection (IBPS). The IBPS, in an effort to enhance exam integrity, conducted a data analysis that uncovered morphed registration photos and the repeated appearance of the same impersonators in interviews and document verification stages.

This modus operandi allowed impersonators to collect joining letters, after which the actual candidates, who had not participated in the process, would join the banks, making detection difficult. The IBPS initiated a re-verification of biometrics, flagging 257 suspects, with 180 already employed in various banks nationwide.

The investigation identified 54 impersonators who appeared for multiple candidates, helping approximately 172 individuals secure bank jobs. The IBPS has debarred these candidates for life and directed banks to take appropriate action. The CBI has filed FIRs naming 135 accused and has arrested four individuals so far, with further arrests anticipated as searches continue.

articles.dek: Demonstrations against the special intensive revision of electoral rolls and Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar continued for a second day, with police detaining hundreds of protesters across the city.
articles.lead: Hundreds of protesters, including political figures and student leaders, were detained by police in Delhi on Sunday as demonstrations against the special intensive revision (SIR) of electoral rolls and Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar persisted. The protests, organized by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), saw activists attempting to march through Connaught Place, a central commercial hub.
articles.takeaway: Demonstrations against the special intensive revision of electoral rolls and Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar continued for a second day, with police detaining hundreds of protesters across the city.
body: Hundreds of protesters, including political figures and student leaders, were detained by police in Delhi on Sunday as demonstrations against the special intensive revision (SIR) of electoral rolls and Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar persisted. The protests, organized by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), saw activists attempting to march through Connaught Place, a central commercial hub.

Despite heavy security deployment and barricading across central Delhi, which aimed to prevent protesters from reaching Jantar Mantar, various student organizations and other groups attempted to mobilize. These groups included the All India Students’ Federation (AISF), the Students’ Federation of India (SFI), the Democratic Youth Federation of India (DYFI), and the Krantikari Yuva Sangathan (KYS).

Protesters marched from Rajiv Chowk Metro station, carrying banners and raising slogans demanding a rollback of the SIR exercise and the resignation of CEC Gyanesh Kumar. Police and the Rapid Action Force detained demonstrators, with some protesters lying on the road and refusing to leave, leading to tense scenes and some sustaining injuries.

As the day progressed, police continued to intercept and detain protesters at various locations, including near Ramakrishna Ashram Marg Metro station and along Panchkuian Road. Journalists covering the demonstrations were also reportedly rounded up. Later in the afternoon, a rally involving around 350 people from several organizations was dispersed by police near Pind Balluchi square.

In parallel, the Krantikari Yuva Sangathan (KYS) organized demonstrations outside the Supreme Court and on the Yamuna River, citing prevention from protesting elsewhere. Some detainees alleged they were taken to a community center in Pandwalan Khurd, approximately 40 km from Connaught Place, without adequate medical assistance or transport. Lawyer Disha Verma alleged that detained protesters were subjected to frisking, had their phones confiscated, and some were allegedly beaten severely during transport.

faqs.answer: Sporadic protests occurred across Delhi, with Connaught Place becoming an epicenter for demonstrations and marches.

articles.dek: The Delhi High Court will hear a plea challenging the closure of Jantar Mantar for protests on October 13, noting the Supreme Court is already handling the matter.
articles.lead: The Delhi High Court has scheduled a hearing for October 13, 2026, regarding a plea that challenges the closure of Jantar Mantar as a site for peace protests. The court declined to hear the matter on October 12, 2026, stating that the Supreme Court is already seized of the issue.
articles.takeaway: The Delhi High Court will hear a plea challenging the closure of Jantar Mantar for protests on October 13, noting the Supreme Court is already handling the matter.
body: The Delhi High Court has scheduled a hearing for October 13, 2026, regarding a plea that challenges the closure of Jantar Mantar as a site for peace protests. The court declined to hear the matter on October 12, 2026, stating that the Supreme Court is already seized of the issue.

During the proceedings, the court also agreed to hear a separate petition alleging that "outsiders" infiltrated a weekend protest and harassed participants. A lawyer brought the matter before a Bench of Acting Chief Justice Nitin Wasudeo Sambre and Justice Sanjay Sharma, arguing that peaceful protests were being suppressed due to the lack of an alternative designated site.

The lawyer emphasized the impact on free speech, stating, "The right to free speech has been quelled to a great extent and that has enormous impact." The court acknowledged the Supreme Court's involvement, noting that the apex court had requested affidavits from the Union government.

"Once the Supreme Court is seized of it, we have to see - to what extent we can look at it again. That’s why let us have it tomorrow," the Bench stated in response to the request for an urgent hearing.

Hundreds had participated in protests on October 10 and 11, called by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), to protest alleged irregularities in the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls by Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.

body: The Delhi Metro Rail Corporation (DMRC) announced that entry and exit services at six metro stations were closed on Monday, October 12, 2026. The closure was in effect from 6 a.m. to 4 p.m. ahead of a planned march by opposition parties to the Supreme Court.

The affected stations include Patel Chowk, Janpath, Rajiv Chowk, Mandi House, Central Secretariat, and Barakhamba Road. The DMRC stated that the situation would be reviewed by security agencies, and updates would be provided accordingly.

Despite the closure of entry and exit points, the interchange facility remained available at all the concerned metro stations. This allowed passengers to transfer between lines without exiting the station.

The opposition's march to the Supreme Court was intended to raise concerns about alleged "vote chori." Congress leaders Rahul Gandhi and Mallikarjun Kharge had sought a meeting with the Chief Justice of India regarding the matter.

Several groups, including the Disha Students’ Organisation, Naujawan Bharat Sabha, and Revolutionary Workers’ Party of India, organized protests at Raj Ghat. Members of these groups reported being picked up and thrown onto the pavement, with one individual sustaining a leg injury and requiring hospitalization. Protesters continued their demonstrations inside the buses, singing songs and discussing alleged irregularities by the Election Commission of India.

At Nangloi, Rajya Sabha member A.A. Rahim initiated 'Jantar Mantar 2.0' and began a hunger strike, demanding action against an inspector for alleged misconduct towards women students and the return of confiscated belongings. Police, however, claimed that officers also sustained injuries during the detentions.

body: Delhi's historic monuments are transforming into venues for a burgeoning cultural economy, hosting events that blend artistic performances with the ambiance of ancient structures. Sites such as Safdarjung Tomb and Purana Qila are now stages for musical evenings, poetry readings, and storytelling sessions, drawing audiences who seek a unique experience beyond traditional auditoriums.

Organizers like Inkpot India and IBTIDA – Ek Mehfil are curating these events, emphasizing the monument itself as a co-star alongside the performers. These gatherings aim to offer attendees an immersive experience, allowing them to connect with history and art in a distinctive setting. The appeal lies in the juxtaposition of contemporary performances against centuries-old architecture, creating an atmosphere difficult to replicate elsewhere.

While the allure of these events is evident, their execution involves navigating complex guidelines from the Archaeological Survey of India (ASI). Initial ASI regulations from 2005 restricted functions at protected sites, favoring classical arts and imposing strict limits on sound, lighting, and crowd size, with a ban on ticketed admissions and commercial activities.

Over time, the ASI has considered allowing more cultural activities, with discussions in 2009 about regular performances at several Delhi monuments. More recently, initiatives like 'Adopt a Heritage 2.0' have invited public and private partnerships to enhance visitor experiences at heritage sites, with organizations designated as 'Smarak Sarthis' to manage these spaces.

Despite the evolving framework, organizers must adhere to ASI's conservation requirements, including strict sound level limits and ensuring events are appropriate for the monument's character and condition. Conservationists stress that the monument's preservation remains paramount, advocating for event scales and types that respect the site's historical and architectural significance.

body: The Bombay High Court has sharply criticized the Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation (BMC) for its inadequate waste management practices across Mumbai. A bench of Justices Girish S Kulkarni and Neela K Gokhale observed that improvements in certain areas, such as South Mumbai, do not reflect a city-wide commitment to cleanliness.

"Everywhere there is filth… Only because Worli is clean or South Mumbai is clean, or Nariman Point is clean, that doesn’t mean entire Mumbai is clean," the court remarked while hearing a plea concerning waste disposal at the Kanjurmarg landfill and garbage dumping on streets and beaches.

Justice Kulkarni expressed a desire for Mumbai to become a city where citizens voluntarily use dustbins, drawing a comparison to practices abroad where deterrents like cameras and penalties encourage proper waste disposal. He noted a lack of such measures in Mumbai.

Despite claims from the BMC's counsel that the situation had improved, the High Court found little progress by ward officers in addressing problematic areas concerning public health and hygiene. The court has requested a comprehensive affidavit detailing the actions taken by ward officers, including measures implemented during the 'Swachhata Abhiyan' on Gandhi Jayanti.

Judges cited personal observations, such as a plastic-strewn hill near a municipal school in Jogeshwari, as evidence of ongoing issues. The court indicated it may summon ward officers from western suburban wards due to reported chaos in waste management and may conduct a second inspection of the Kanjurmarg facility.
The court will also address complaints regarding odor and environmental pollution from the Kanjurmarg site at the next hearing on October 22.

body: The Bombay High Court has directed the Maharashtra government to take measures to restore the confidence of students protesting the Maharashtra Public Service Commission (MPSC) recruitment process. A Division Bench, hearing a petition concerning public inconvenience caused by the protests in Pune, urged students to return to their studies while the matter is under judicial review.

Students have been protesting alleged procedural irregularities and paper leaks in MPSC examinations, leading to road blockades in Pune. The court acknowledged that these protests indicated genuine grievances that required attention, noting the significant number of government job vacancies.

The Maharashtra government informed the court that it had agreed to set examination fees at ₹100 and to conduct exams in person. The state also mentioned that a representation regarding the MPSC Chairperson's resignation had been sent to the Governor.

The High Court emphasized that students come to Pune for education and are not anti-national. It requested the state to provide written details on the recruitment process and departmental vacancies, issuing a notice and requiring an affidavit. The court also advised students to seek permission for protests and to conduct them in designated areas without disrupting public life.

Calling for peace, the court stressed that no negative message should emanate from Pune, a prominent educational hub. It urged students to resume attending classes and requested the state to consider the concerns of parents whose children are pursuing education in the city. The court also noted that the police had exercised restraint during the protests.

body: Delhi Police have launched a localized outreach campaign to discourage public participation in a protest scheduled for October 10 at Jantar Mantar. The demonstration, organized by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) along with youth groups, aims to demand the immediate removal of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar and the suspension of the special intensive revision (SIR) drive. Permission for the protest has been officially denied by the authorities.

Police are engaging with student accommodation providers, market associations, and resident welfare groups to appeal to citizens to refrain from joining the agitation between October 7 and 10. Meetings are being held to emphasize the importance of maintaining law and order, with police stating that participation could worsen the situation in the New Delhi district. While acknowledging the fundamental right to protest, officials noted constitutional limitations.

Local shopkeepers have been asked to close their establishments by 11:30 p.m. instead of midnight. Social activist Mohammad Shahid Gangohi, who attended a security briefing, stated that citizens were advised not to join the crowds. He also cautioned against the repetition of forceful tactics used by police in July, referencing an incident where officers allegedly interfered with a local sweet shop.

CJP leader Saurav Das criticized the restrictions, asserting that administrative pressure would not deter demonstrators and that intimidation tactics would no longer be effective. The police are conducting targeted briefings at colleges, universities, and student housing areas to curb mobilization.

Authorities are monitoring individuals who participated in previous demonstrations and have issued orders for potential pre-emptive detention under Sections 126 and 170 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS). Security agencies plan to use Facial Recognition System (FRS) technology to track over 2,800 individuals flagged during earlier protests.
